1.title: Document Frame: language and metadata
1.description: A browser needs a document type and a clear head before it can present a page reliably. Complete the starter so it declares English, UTF-8, the title “Trail Notes”, and one main landmark.
1.learningObjective: Build a valid HTML document frame with a language, character encoding, title, and body.
instructions: Keep `<!doctype html>` as the first declaration.
Set `lang="en"` on the root `html` element.
Put a UTF-8 charset and the page title inside `head`.
Place the visible heading inside one `main` element in `body`.

workedExample.output: A document titled “Trail Notes” with one main heading.
workedExample.explanation: The doctype selects standards mode. A root language helps assistive technology choose pronunciation, while UTF-8 supports a broad range of text.

1.hint: The title belongs in the document head; the heading belongs in the body.
1.explanation: The doctype selects standards mode. A root language helps assistive technology choose pronunciation, while UTF-8 supports a broad range of text.

testCases.description: Declare the HTML doctype before the root element.
Set the document language to English and the character set to UTF-8.
Place “Trail Notes” in the title element.
Use one main landmark for the visible page content.

1.expectedOutput: Trail Notes
1.expectedOutputHint: Visual reference only. The HTML preview is rendered in a sandbox; completion is reviewed against source requirements, not browser-executed tests.
1.starterCode:
<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
  <!-- Add the language, charset, and title. -->
</head>
<body>
  <!-- Add the main page content. -->
</body>
</html>

2.title: Heading Ladder: a clear page outline
2.description: Turn the supplied page outline into a readable article: “Build a Better Bookmark” is the page heading, “Choose a destination” and “Save the page” are sections, and “Use a descriptive name” belongs under the saving section.
2.learningObjective: Use heading levels to expose a logical outline without skipping levels for visual sizing.
instructions: Use one `h1` for the article title.
Use `h2` for both main sections.
Use `h3` for the nested naming tip.
Keep the headings in the same order as the content they introduce.

workedExample.output: h1 → h2 → h3, in that order.
workedExample.explanation: Heading levels communicate hierarchy to browsers and assistive technology. CSS can change the visual size without changing the semantic level.

2.hint: Choose each heading by its place in the outline, not by the font size you want.
2.explanation: Heading levels communicate hierarchy to browsers and assistive technology. CSS can change the visual size without changing the semantic level.

testCases.description: Use exactly one h1 for “Build a Better Bookmark”.
Mark “Choose a destination” and “Save the page” as h2 headings.
Nest “Use a descriptive name” under the saving section as an h3.
Do not skip from h1 directly to h3.

2.expectedOutput:
Build a Better Bookmark

Choose a destination

Open the page you want to keep.

Save the page

Use a descriptive name

A useful name makes the bookmark easy to find.
2.expectedOutputHint: Visual reference only. The HTML preview is rendered in a sandbox; completion is reviewed against source requirements, not browser-executed tests.

3.title: Emphasis in Context: strong and em
3.description: Write a short safety note. Mark “save your work” as especially important and “before closing the tab” as emphasized timing. Keep both phrases inside one paragraph.
3.learningObjective: Use semantic emphasis to mark important meaning rather than styling text with presentational tags.
instructions: Create one paragraph for the note.
Wrap “save your work” in `strong`.
Wrap “before closing the tab” in `em`.
Keep the sentence readable when the emphasis styling is removed.

workedExample.input: A sentence with a key action and timing
workedExample.output: The action is strong; the timing is emphasized.
workedExample.explanation: Semantic emphasis communicates meaning to assistive technology and search tools. It is more useful than choosing a tag only because it looks bold or italic.

3.hint: `strong` communicates importance; `em` adds stress that can affect the sentence meaning.
3.explanation: Semantic emphasis communicates meaning to assistive technology and search tools. It is more useful than choosing a tag only because it looks bold or italic.

testCases.description: Use one paragraph for the safety note.
Wrap “save your work” in a strong element.
Wrap “before closing the tab” in an em element.
Do not use b or i as replacements for the requested meaning.

3.expectedOutput: Remember to save your work before closing the tab.
3.expectedOutputHint: Visual reference only. The HTML preview is rendered in a sandbox; completion is reviewed against source requirements, not browser-executed tests.

4.title: Link Labels: describe the destination
4.description: Add a link to the public course guide at `/learn`. Its label should tell the learner that the destination contains course tracks, not say “click here”.
4.learningObjective: Create a link whose visible text explains where it leads.
instructions: Use an anchor element with `href="/learn"`.
Write “Explore the course tracks” as the link text.
Place the link after a short sentence introducing the guide.
Do not use an empty anchor or a bare URL as its label.

workedExample.output: A named link: “Explore the course tracks”.
workedExample.explanation: Descriptive link text gives context in a list of links and helps all readers predict the destination before opening it.

4.hint: A person navigating by links should understand the destination from the label alone.
4.explanation: Descriptive link text gives context in a list of links and helps all readers predict the destination before opening it.

testCases.description: Point the anchor to `/learn`.
Use the exact descriptive label “Explore the course tracks”.
Keep the link inside the page’s main content.
Include a sentence that introduces the guide.

4.expectedOutput:
Keep learning

Choose a topic for your next practice session.

Explore the course tracks

5.title: Image Description: meaningful alternative text
5.description: Add the local Game Trail mark to the page. Give it alternative text that identifies the mark, and keep the visible heading meaningful if the image is unavailable.
5.learningObjective: Provide concise alternative text that conveys the purpose of an informative image.
instructions: Use `/assets/Game-in-my-style.png` as the image source.
Set `alt="Game Trail emblem"` because the image identifies the brand.
Keep the text heading “Practice coding by playing”.
Do not use a filename or “image” as the alternative text.

workedExample.explanation: Alternative text provides an equivalent for people who cannot see the image and appears when the image resource fails to load.

5.hint: Describe the information the image adds, not how pixels look.
5.explanation: Alternative text provides an equivalent for people who cannot see the image and appears when the image resource fails to load.

testCases.description: Use the supplied local image path.
Provide the exact informative alt text “Game Trail emblem”.
Keep the heading visible as real text.
Do not leave the informative image with an empty alt value.

5.expectedOutput: Practice coding by playing
5.expectedOutputHint: Visual reference only. The HTML preview is rendered in a sandbox; completion is reviewed against source requirements, not browser-executed tests.

6.title: Task List: ordered steps and unordered supplies
6.description: Create a small “Pack for a coding meetup” page with three supplies and three preparation steps. Supplies can be in any order; the preparation steps must stay numbered.
6.learningObjective: Choose ordered and unordered lists according to whether the item sequence matters.
instructions: Use a `ul` for the three supplies.
Use an `ol` for the three preparation steps.
Put every item in an `li` element.
Give each list a nearby heading.

workedExample.output: Unordered supply list + numbered preparation list.
workedExample.explanation: Ordered lists encode a sequence or ranking. Unordered lists group related items where order does not matter.

6.hint: Ask whether reordering the items changes their meaning: that determines the list type.
6.explanation: Ordered lists encode a sequence or ranking. Unordered lists group related items where order does not matter.

testCases.description: Group three supplies in one unordered list.
Group three preparation steps in one ordered list.
Use list items for every entry.
Add a heading before each list.

6.expectedOutput:
Pack for a coding meetup

Supplies

  • Laptop
  • Charger
  • Notebook

Preparation

  1. Save current work
  2. Charge the laptop
  3. Bring the project notes
6.expectedOutputHint: Visual reference only. The HTML preview is rendered in a sandbox; completion is reviewed against source requirements, not browser-executed tests.

7.title: Quote Source: cite the speaker
7.description: Present a short quote from the project mentor. Use `blockquote` for the quoted passage and a separate citation line that names the speaker.
7.learningObjective: Mark a multi-sentence quotation with blockquote and identify its source in nearby text.
instructions: Place the two-sentence quotation inside `blockquote`.
Write the quote exactly as shown in the expected example.
Add a paragraph after the quote that names “Project mentor”.
Do not use quotation marks as a substitute for the blockquote element.

workedExample.input: A multi-sentence quotation plus its speaker
workedExample.output: A blockquote followed by a source paragraph.
workedExample.explanation: blockquote represents an extended quotation. A nearby attribution makes the source understandable without relying on visual styling.

7.hint: The quote and its attribution have different roles, so keep them in distinct elements.
7.explanation: blockquote represents an extended quotation. A nearby attribution makes the source understandable without relying on visual styling.

testCases.description: Use blockquote for the full two-sentence passage.
Include both sentences in their original order.
Identify the speaker in a following paragraph.
Keep the quotation inside the main content.

7.expectedOutput:
A note for learners

Small steps make difficult ideas easier to practice. Every clear error is another clue.

— Project mentor

8.title: Page Landmarks: header, nav, main, footer
8.description: Build a compact course page with a site header, a navigation list, one main area, and a footer. The navigation should point to the “Lessons” section.
8.learningObjective: Use page landmarks to give navigation, primary content, and supporting information distinct roles.
instructions: Place the site name in `header`.
Put a descriptive link inside `nav`.
Use one `main` element for the lesson heading and summary.
Place the copyright note in `footer`.

workedExample.output: Four distinct landmarks with navigation to `#lessons`.
workedExample.explanation: Landmarks help people move through a page using assistive technology and make the document structure easier to scan.

8.hint: Use each landmark for its page-level purpose; do not wrap every element in a generic div.
8.explanation: Landmarks help people move through a page using assistive technology and make the document structure easier to scan.

testCases.description: Use header, nav, main, and footer elements.
Link the navigation item to `#lessons`.
Put the lesson summary inside a section with id `lessons`.
Do not create more than one main landmark.

9.title: Data Table: label columns and rows
9.description: Show three practice sessions with their topic and duration. Use a caption, semantic table sections, and column headers that are associated with the values below them.
9.learningObjective: Build a small data table with a caption, a header group, and scoped column headings.
instructions: Add a caption that describes the table.
Put the column labels in `thead` and use `th scope="col"`.
Put the three session records in `tbody`.
Use one row per session and keep topic and duration in separate cells.

workedExample.input: Three session records with two fields each
workedExample.output: A captioned table with scoped headers and three body rows.
workedExample.explanation: Captions describe a table before it is read. Scoped headers help assistive technology connect each cell with its column label.

9.hint: A table is for relationships between data values, not for positioning page sections.
9.explanation: Captions describe a table before it is read. Scoped headers help assistive technology connect each cell with its column label.

testCases.description: Provide a descriptive caption.
Use thead with two column headers scoped to columns.
Use tbody with three data rows.
Include topic and duration in separate data cells.

10.title: Form Labels: connect each field to its name
10.description: Build a sign-up form for a weekly coding reminder. Ask for an email address and an optional display name. Each input must have a visible label and a stable matching id.
10.learningObjective: Create a short form whose visible labels are programmatically associated with their inputs.
instructions: Wrap the fields in a form with a clear heading.
Give the email input `type="email"`, `id="email"`, and `required`.
Associate a visible “Email address” label with `email`.
Add an optional text field with a matching `display-name` label and id.

workedExample.input: Two form fields: required email and optional display name
workedExample.output: Both controls have visible, associated labels.
workedExample.explanation: Visible labels communicate a field’s purpose and enlarge its clickable target. An email input also gives browsers a useful input mode and basic format handling.

10.hint: The label `for` value must exactly match its input id.
10.explanation: Visible labels communicate a field’s purpose and enlarge its clickable target. An email input also gives browsers a useful input mode and basic format handling.

testCases.description: Use one form and one heading.
Use a required email input with id `email`.
Connect the “Email address” label to the email input.
Provide an optional display-name input with a matching visible label.

10.expectedOutput: Weekly coding reminder
10.expectedOutputHint: Visual reference only. The HTML preview is rendered in a sandbox; completion is reviewed against source requirements, not browser-executed tests.
